descriptions: she who devours (kalana) Mahākāla, the devourer of all beings; the beginning of all (Mahānirvāṇa 4.31-32)
black because every colour disappears in black as all beings enter Kālī (Mahānirvāṇa 13.5-6)
pure consciousness, witness of all, watching Time play (Mahānirvāṇa 13.12)
the Śakti without whom Sadāśiva is a corpse (Toḍala 1.25)
negations: formless (arūpā): her form is imagined according to her qualities and acts (Mahānirvāṇa 5.140)
the formless meditation on her is beyond speech and mind (Mahānirvāṇa 5.137-138)
relation_to_self: The worshipper is to see all as Brahman ('sarvaṃ brahmamayam', Mahānirvāṇa 3.120, 8.175); in the devotional Kālī tradition the self is her child, and in the Kaula view the bound jīva is Śiva himself (Kulārṇava 9.42).
relation_to_world: The worlds arise from her and return into her as colours into black; she creates, sustains and devours, and is the Mother of Time (Mahānirvāṇa 5.140; 13.5-8).
caveat: The Kālī tantras make the Goddess the source of Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (Nirvāṇa Tantra) and treat Viṣṇu's avatāras as her forms (Toḍala 10); they accept a one-truth reading only with her as that truth. The devotional tradition resists dissolving her motherhood into an impersonal absolute.

descriptions: Śiva, the supreme Brahman, partless, all-knowing, the doer of all, pure, non-dual, self-luminous, without beginning or end, without qualities, being–consciousness–bliss (Kulārṇava 1.7-8)
the bliss (ānanda) born of the union of Śakti and Śiva is called liberation (Kulārṇava 5.79)
bliss is the form of Brahman, and it abides in the body (Kulārṇava 5.80)
relation_to_self: The individual souls are parts of Śiva like sparks of a fire, covered by beginningless ignorance (Kulārṇava 1.8-9); bound by fetters the self is jīva, freed it is Sadāśiva (Kulārṇava 9.42-43).
relation_to_world: Kula is Śakti — the totality of powers and of the manifest — and Akula is Śiva; the Kaula joins both (Kulārṇava 17.27).
caveat: The Kaula texts refuse to be classed as dualist or non-dualist (Kulārṇava 1.110) and insist that the truth is realised through the guru's transmission and Kula practice, not by learning (1.96-100); a purely doctrinal one-truth reading leaves out the ritual and lineage conditions they make essential.

descriptions: the supreme power of knowledge, will and action, straight as a line and again coiled like a sleeping serpent, the power of sound (Kubjikāmata 2.2, hymn)
the supreme primal yoni of the supreme, fourfold as beyond form, form, word and body (Kubjikāmata 11.6-7)
dark as collyrium, bent, both beautiful and deformed, of many forms (Kubjikāmata 2.4-5)
negations: beyond form (rūpātīta) at its highest level (Kubjikāmata 11.7)
relation_to_self: The Goddess is the coiled power within the practitioner's body, located in the six centres; the initiate receives her command (ājñā) through the guru lineage.
relation_to_world: The world is born within the sixfold order of the Goddess (Kubjikāmata 11.13-16); Bhairava and she are cause and effect of one another (2.17-18).
caveat: The Kubjikā ultimate is expressed through a secret mantra-maṇḍala system and lineage command; the tradition treats this knowledge as unshareable outside initiation, so any one-truth equation is at most an outer reading.

descriptions: Kāmākhyā is dharma, artha, kāma and liberation; nothing in the three worlds exists without her (Kāmākhyā Tantra 1.9-13)
the subtle root-nature (mūla-prakṛti) who divided herself into māyā and vidyā to bring about creation (Bṛhaddharma Purāṇa madhya 6.98-124)
the Mother (Mā) of the devotional songs, both terrible and tender
negations: herself without the three guṇas, she shines through the one who has them (Bṛhaddharma madhya 6.120)
relation_to_self: The devotee is her child; the digests adopt the Kaula and Vedāntic teaching that the self is one with the Goddess.
relation_to_world: The earth bears her body in the pīṭhas, where the parts of Satī fell (Kālikā Purāṇa 18.40-50).
caveat: Devotional Bengal Śāktism keeps the relation of child and Mother and resists merging it into an impersonal absolute; ritual texts of the same region keep sharp distinctions of eligibility (caste, bhāva) that a one-truth reading should not erase.
